title: Compare and Contrast Network Access and Management Methods

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Administrators need secure ways to connect sites and users and to manage network systems. Identify who connects, how the connection works, and whether management uses production connectivity or a separate path.
bullets: Site-to-site, client-to-site, and clientless VPN access
SSH, GUI, API, and console management
sections.callout: CONNECT SITES → CONNECT USERS → MANAGE DEVICES → CONTROL ADMIN ACCESS → KEEP A BACKUP PATH

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Given a remote-access or device-management scenario, identify who is connecting, how the connection is made, and whether management traffic uses the production network or an independent path.
bullets: Browser access without a traditional client → Clientless
Corporate traffic only through VPN → Split tunnel
All client traffic through VPN → Full tunnel

sections.title: VPN Connection Types

entries.title: Site-to-Site VPN
paragraphs: A site-to-site VPN securely connects two networks across an untrusted network. Users at headquarters and a branch can communicate through a persistent network-to-network tunnel without establishing individual sessions.

entries.title: Client-to-Site VPN
paragraphs: A client-to-site VPN connects an individual endpoint or remote worker to an organization's network.

entries.title: Clientless VPN
paragraphs: A clientless VPN provides remote access without a traditional installed VPN client, often through a web browser or built-in capability.
entries.memoryHook: Remote access without installing a full client.

sections.callout: Site-to-site describes network-to-network. Client-to-site describes endpoint-to-network. Clientless describes how the endpoint accesses the service.

entries.title: Split Tunnel
paragraphs: Only selected traffic, such as corporate destinations, enters the VPN; other traffic exits through the client's local Internet connection. This reduces VPN bandwidth but creates simultaneous trusted and untrusted paths.

entries.title: Full Tunnel
paragraphs: All client traffic, including ordinary Internet traffic, enters the corporate VPN so centralized controls can inspect and govern it.

sections.title: Connection Methods

entries.title: Secure Shell (SSH)
paragraphs: SSH provides encrypted remote command-line administration for routers, switches, servers, and other devices.

entries.title: Graphical User Interface (GUI)
paragraphs: A GUI provides visual menus, buttons, forms, and dashboards for human administrators.

entries.title: Application Programming Interface (API)
paragraphs: An API lets software manage another system programmatically and supports automation, orchestration, scripting, and integration.

entries.title: Console
paragraphs: A console connection provides direct device management and remains valuable when the device has no IP configuration or production networking is broken.

sections.callout: Remote commands → SSH. Human visual control → GUI. Automation → API. Direct device access → Console.

sections.title: Jump Box / Jump Host
paragraphs: A jump box is a hardened, controlled intermediary through which administrators connect before reaching sensitive systems. It centralizes access control, reduces management exposure, supports logging, and preserves security segmentation.
examples: Administrator laptop → Jump host → Server or network device
Remote administrator → VPN → Jump box → Router
sections.callout: A VPN provides secure connectivity; a jump box controls the administrative path inside the network.

sections.title: In-Band and Out-of-Band Management

entries.title: In-Band Management
paragraphs: In-band management uses the normal production network—for example, SSH, GUI, or API access over production IP connectivity. If production fails, remote management may also fail.
entries.memoryHook: Manage the network through the network.

entries.title: Out-of-Band Management
paragraphs: Out-of-band management uses an independent management path, such as a dedicated network, management interface, or console-server system. It can remain available during production outages.

sections.callout: Console is a direct device-management method. Out-of-band describes a broader separate management architecture; console access can be part of it.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Remote user to organization → Client-to-site VPN
Only corporate traffic through VPN → Split tunnel
All traffic through VPN → Full tunnel

entries.title: Site-to-Site vs. Client-to-Site
paragraphs: Network to network → Site-to-site. Device or user to network → Client-to-site.

entries.title: Clientless vs. Client-to-Site
paragraphs: Client-to-site describes the endpoint-to-network relationship. Clientless describes access without a traditional installed VPN client; these are not opposites.

entries.title: Split vs. Full Tunnel
paragraphs: Corporate traffic only → Split. Everything → Full.

entries.title: SSH vs. Console
paragraphs: Remote network CLI → SSH. Direct device access, especially when networking is broken → Console.

entries.title: GUI vs. API
paragraphs: Human visual interaction → GUI. Software automation and integration → API.

entries.title: Jump Box vs. VPN
paragraphs: Secure transport into a network → VPN. Controlled administrative intermediary → Jump box.

entries.title: Console vs. Out-of-Band
paragraphs: Direct local method → Console. Separate management architecture or path → Out-of-band.

entries.title: In-Band vs. Out-of-Band
paragraphs: Production network → In-band. Separate management path → Out-of-band.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Some traffic through VPN → Split tunnel
All traffic through VPN → Full tunnel
sections.callout: CONNECT SITES → CONNECT USERS → MANAGE DEVICES → CONTROL ADMIN ACCESS → KEEP A BACKUP PATH
